value.overview: The Blue-and-gold Tanager (Bangsia arcaei) is a small, colorful tanager of the Talamancan highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama. It inhabits humid mountain forests, forest edges, and areas with dense vegetation, usually at middle to high elevations. Its bright blue and yellow plumage makes it a distinctive member of the tanager family, although it can be difficult to observe in thick montane forest. It is strongly associated with cool, wet highland environments.
value.classification: The Blue-and-gold Tanager belongs to the tanager family, Thraupidae, and the genus Bangsia. It is closely associated with other highland tanagers of Central and northern South America.
value.identification: This tanager is recognized by its contrasting blue and golden-yellow plumage. The head and upperparts are mainly rich blue, while the underparts and lower body are yellow to golden yellow. Darker markings around the face and wings add contrast, and the bill is short and conical, suited to a mixed diet. Sexes are generally similar in appearance. It is usually detected by movement and calls within dense, humid mountain vegetation rather than by prolonged views.
value.rangeHabitat: The Blue-and-gold Tanager has a restricted range in the Talamancan mountain region of Costa Rica and adjacent western Panama. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly in the highlands of the Cordillera de Talamanca and other suitable montane areas, including protected mountain forests. It uses humid evergreen forest, cloud forest, forest borders, and dense second growth, generally at middle and upper elevations. Preservation of connected highland forest is important because its range is geographically limited.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a resident species in Costa Rica and does not undertake regular long-distance migration. Local or seasonal movements along mountain slopes may occur, but reliable evidence for a consistent migratory pattern is limited.
value.breeding: The breeding biology of the Blue-and-gold Tanager is not as well documented as that of many widespread tanagers. Breeding is associated with humid montane forest in its restricted Central American range. Like related tanagers, it is expected to build a small cup-shaped nest in vegetation and to lay a small clutch, with both adults likely involved in feeding the young. Detailed information on nest sites, incubation, and nesting success remains limited.
value.dietFeeding: The Blue-and-gold Tanager feeds on a mixture of fruit, berries, and arthropods. It forages in trees and dense vegetation, often taking small fruits and searching foliage for insects and other invertebrates. Its feeding habits may help disperse seeds while also contributing to the control of small insect populations. It can join mixed-species feeding flocks in montane forest, especially when moving through the middle and upper layers of vegetation.
value.behavior: This species is generally active and inconspicuous, moving through dense mountain forest in search of food. It may occur alone, in pairs, or in mixed-species flocks with other highland birds. Its movements are usually quick, and it often remains partly concealed by foliage. Vocal activity and brief flashes of blue and yellow can reveal its presence. It is most likely to be encountered along forest trails, edges, and other locations where vegetation provides both food and cover.

conservation.populationTrend: The population trend is not fully known, but habitat loss and fragmentation in highland forests may be causing localized declines.
conservation.threats: The principal concerns are clearance and fragmentation of montane forest for agriculture, livestock production, roads, and other development. Climate change may also reduce or shift the extent of suitable cool, wet highland habitat. Because the species has a limited range, the loss of connected forest in Costa Rica or Panama could have disproportionate effects.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore high-elevation cloud forest and other native montane habitats in Costa Rica, especially within and between protected areas. Maintaining forest corridors, supporting sustainable land use near highland reserves, and reducing further fragmentation can benefit this species and other Talamancan birds. Bird monitoring in Costa Rican mountain forests is also valuable for detecting population changes.
